In “in the ovarian cancer population,” “activation of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein,” or “the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein,” the article or preposition introduces a larger noun phrase headed by a non-disease noun. Decide the label from what a disease-denoting noun phrase refers to in context, not from the category-like meaning of its head noun.

**Label as Disease Class** when: - the phrase is a superordinate category reference that enumerates or classifies kinds of disease (introduced by “such as,” “including,” “types of,” or a class-membership frame, e.g., “is an autosomal recessive disease”)

quotes.quote: **IF** a candidate **Specific Disease** span is a disease-like head noun extended by qualifiers (laterality, inheritance or carrier status, extent, or severity), by a prepositional complement naming a molecule, gene product, or anatomical structure, or by a parenthetical or appositive that restates a disease already named in the text, - **THEN** tag only the compact, fixed nomenclature unit (eponym, abbreviation, or head-final compound) that the text uses as the disease’s name. Exclude the qualifiers and complement.

note: Anaphoric anchoring is not among the listed 1.1 anchors; quoted the referential-scope principle.

quotes.quote: **Label as Specific Disease** when the phrase is anchored to one individuated condition, either: - by a proper name, eponym, acronym, gene, or pathogen identity (e.g., “Norrie disease,” “G6PD deficiency,” “C7 deficiency”), or - by a patient-level clinical role, meaning it is the argument of a predicate that expresses a specific patient’s presentation, diagnosis, or finding (e.g., “presenting with,” “found to have,” “diagnosed with,” “affected by,” or a patient “with” a condition).

**IF** a candidate **Specific Disease** span is a disease-like head noun extended by qualifiers (laterality, inheritance or carrier status, extent, or severity), by a prepositional complement naming a molecule, gene product, or anatomical structure, or by a parenthetical or appositive that restates a disease already named in the text, - **THEN** tag only the compact, fixed nomenclature unit (eponym, abbreviation, or head-final compound) that the text uses as the disease’s name. Exclude the qualifiers and complement.

Do NOT trim when the full span is an established, fixed name, including: - an eponym followed by a disease-type head noun, even with internal modifiers (e.g., “Sjogren-Larsson syndrome,” “Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome,” “Coats disease”); - a head-final compound whose non-head element is an identifier or proper name (e.g., “Coats telangiectasis,” “G6PD deficiency”);
quotes.condition_words: a head-final compound whose non-head element is an identifier or proper name
